material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
public_task.research_goal: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Campaign hypotheses

**H1 [tentative]** Under dossier contact conditions, X2 should give the largest single-contact target recovery into the organic phase, while X0 may give higher purity but much lower recovery. This assumes the nominal extractant mapping is reliable. Test by holding reaction and contact conditions fixed and comparing final organic-phase assays.

**H2 [tentative]** Reaction outcome likely depends strongly on anonymous catalyst, temperature, and time; initially screen catalyst categories under a common moderate condition. A catalyst result will only be generalized within the tested recipe, and a later result could overturn it.

**Decision rule (prospective):** prioritize final materials meeting purity >=0.80; among those, choose the highest observed recovery, treating small unreplicated differences as unresolved. Use the 12 shared intermediate measurements mainly to diagnose reaction progress or phase selection.

# Campaign hypotheses

**H1 [partly supported]** X2 remains the working extractant based on the dossier and is adequate to produce an organic final material, but its actual recovery advantage over other X categories is untested. The nominal mapping could still be wrong.

**H2 [supported only for tested recipe]** At 350 K for 3600 s in S0 with equal 0.018 mol charges, C3 gave the strongest pre-extraction HPLC profile among C1–C3 and the only clearly specification-passing final assay: batch 4 purity 0.8395, recovery 0.0428 (events runner-operation-0059 and -0070). C1 was near the threshold (batch 2 purity 0.7948, recovery 0.0391; events -0025/-0036), while C2 was poorer (batch 3 purity 0.5410; events -0042/-0053). C0 under a different, harsher/time-varying treatment was poor and therefore not a clean comparator.

**H3 [tentative]** With C3, recovery may improve by reducing wash volume while retaining purity >=0.80, and by finding a reaction temperature/time or solvent with greater target yield. Test smaller wash and reaction-condition/solvent variations. Small final-assay differences will remain unresolved without replication.

**Decision rule:** recommend the highest observed recovery among batches with final purity >=0.80. Current provisional choice is batch 4; replace it if a later batch passes purity and has materially higher observed recovery.

# Campaign hypotheses — final source-stage synthesis

**H1 [not supported as a general process claim]** The dossier suggested X2 would give the best extraction recovery and X0 the cleanest organic phase. X2 was workable, but the X0 comparison in batch 8 did not improve final purity (0.4878) despite a strong S1 reaction feed (events runner-operation-0127 and -0138). Because reaction feeds and wash conditions were not identical to all X2 batches, extractant rankings beyond these tested combinations remain unresolved.

**H2 [supported in the tested S0 recipe]** C3 was the best catalyst category screened at 350 K/3600 s: batch 4 achieved final purity 0.8395 and recovery 0.0428 (events runner-operation-0059 and -0070), whereas C1 was just below specification and C2 was substantially lower purity (events -0025/-0036 and -0042/-0053). C0 was tested under a non-comparable harsher sequence and is not cleanly ranked.

**H3 [mixed / narrowed]** Lower-temperature, longer C3 reactions often increased pre-extraction HPLC yield, and S1/S2 raised it further (e.g. events runner-operation-0110 and -0144), but their final products remained below purity 0.80. Changing or repeating washes did not reliably rescue purity and could reduce recovery; batch-to-batch process variation and differing feeds confound a precise wash-volume effect. Thus the higher-recovery sub-specification results are not candidates for the stated objective.

**Final decision:** batch 4 is the only observed batch clearly meeting purity >=0.80 (0.8395) and has recovery 0.0428. Recommend it despite modest recovery, because the prospective rule prioritizes specification before recovery. Batch 2 at 0.7948 is below the threshold, and all later higher-recovery batches also fail purity. This choice would change if a repeat of another recipe were shown to meet >=0.80 purity with higher recovery.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic interpretation

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–liquid extraction–washing–solvent-removal process. The final recovery is not controlled by any single operation: it is approximately the product of reaction yield, extraction retention, washing retention, and handling retention. Purity is instead governed by the relative survival of target and impurities through those same stages. A recipe can therefore produce a relatively large amount of target at the reaction stage yet fail because its impurities follow the target through purification.

A useful conceptual mass balance is

n_target,final ≈ n_charge × Y_reaction × f_extract,target × f_wash,target × f_handling,target,

and

purity_final ≈ n_target,final /(n_target,final + n_impurity,final).

Here the factors are effective quantities rather than separately identified parameters. The campaign did not directly measure absolute species amounts at every stage, and the HPLC and final-assay metrics have different stage-specific contracts. Consequently, I do not treat a final-assay conversion value as a continuation of the earlier HPLC conversion measurement or fit a detailed kinetic model by equating them.

## Reaction stage

The important reaction variables appeared to be catalyst category, solvent category, temperature, and heating duration. Catalyst and solvent effects were strongly coupled: a catalyst ranking established in S0 should not automatically be extrapolated to another solvent.

The clearest catalyst comparison used S0 at 350 K for 3600 s, equal 0.018 mol reagent/component charges, and otherwise similar X2 workups:

- Batch 2, C1: reaction-stage HPLC conversion 0.1817, yield 0.0916, selectivity 0.4872 and purity 0.5378. Final purity was 0.7948 and recovery 0.0391.
- Batch 3, C2: HPLC conversion 0.2329 but yield only 0.0481, selectivity 0.2298 and purity 0.2429. Final purity was 0.5410 and recovery 0.0268.
- Batch 4, C3: HPLC conversion 0.1872, yield 0.0910, selectivity 0.5559 and purity 0.5938. Final purity was 0.8395 and recovery 0.0428.

Thus conversion alone was not a useful objective. C2 had the highest observed conversion of these three batches but converted material much less selectively. C3 supplied the cleanest reaction mixture and ultimately the only final material clearly satisfying purity ≥0.80. Within this tested S0 condition, I infer that C3 favors the target pathway relative to the impurity pathway.

Batch 1 used C0, but it is not a clean member of that comparison. It had a larger 0.04 + 0.04 mol charge and sequential heating at 350 K for 1800 s followed by 360 K for 7200 s. Its early HPLC result was poor (conversion 0.1116, yield 0.0376 and selectivity 0.3877), and its final purity and recovery were only 0.3036 and 0.0085. This is evidence that the complete batch-1 recipe was poor, not proof that C0 is intrinsically the worst catalyst under every condition.

At C3, lowering the temperature from 350 K/3600 s to 330 K/7200 s in S0 raised the observed reaction-stage yield from 0.0910 in batch 4 to about 0.128–0.130 in batches 5, 6 and 12. Their HPLC selectivities remained similar, 0.538–0.551. This suggests a kinetic tradeoff: the longer, cooler treatment generated more target while retaining reasonable reaction selectivity. A plausible qualitative model is competing target and impurity pathways,

R → P with rate kP(T, catalyst, solvent),
R → I with rate kI(T, catalyst, solvent),
P → D as a possible slower degradation pathway,

where each rate constant could have Arrhenius-like temperature dependence. The data do not determine those constants, reaction orders, or even whether the network is truly irreversible. The observation merely supports different effective pathway ratios under different recipes.

There was substantial run-to-run variation. Nominally related S0/C3/330 K/7200 s batches 5, 6 and 12 gave HPLC conversions of 0.2805, 0.2437 and 0.2108. Their yields were much more consistent, 0.1282, 0.1296 and 0.1297, but recovery-like HPLC fields varied from 0.1044 to 0.1374. Some variation may be analytical noise, while some may be process variation. Because workup details also differed, it is not possible to infer precise repeatability or a kinetic rate law.

## Solvent effects

With C3 at 330 K for 7200 s, solvent category changed reaction behavior markedly:

- S0 batches gave HPLC yields near 0.129 and selectivities near 0.54–0.55.
- S1 gave much higher HPLC yields: 0.2154 in batch 7 and 0.2385 in batch 8, with conversions near 0.44. Selectivities were 0.5066 and 0.4905.
- S2 gave HPLC yields 0.2355 in batch 9 and 0.2071 in batch 10, conversions 0.4405 and 0.4359, and selectivities 0.5158 and 0.5372.
- S3 was unfavorable: batch 11 gave yield 0.1124, selectivity 0.2067 and HPLC purity 0.2612.

I therefore infer that S1 and S2 accelerate or enable greater overall conversion relative to S0, but they do not suppress impurity formation enough for the tested workups. S3 appears to favor non-target chemistry. These are categorical observations; the anonymous solvent identities prevent attributing them to polarity, coordination, acidity, or another real molecular property.

The key coupling is that the solvent producing the most target was not the solvent producing the best final material. Batch 9 (S2) had reaction-stage yield 0.2355 and final recovery 0.0969, the highest final recovery observed, but final purity was only 0.6652. Batch 7 (S1) reached final recovery 0.0788 but purity only 0.5742. In contrast, batch 4 (S0) had lower reaction-stage yield yet final purity 0.8395. This is consistent with S1/S2 increasing both target and co-produced impurities.

## Extraction model

The material dossier supplied nominal distribution coefficients. For a single equilibrium contact, a natural prior model is

fP,org = KP Vorg /(Vaq + KP Vorg),
fI,org = KI Vorg /(Vaq + KI Vorg),

with enrichment controlled by fP,org/fI,org. The dossier suggested X2 had the largest product partition coefficient and X0 a potentially useful selectivity ratio. I used X2 for most batches because it should retain more target in the organic phase.

The experimental evidence only partly supports that prior. Batch 8 tested X0 after an S1 reaction and used a 0.04 L wash. Although its pre-workup HPLC yield was high (0.2385), its final recovery was only 0.0331 and purity was 0.4878. The related S1/X2 batch 7 had final recovery 0.0788 and purity 0.5742. This result did not demonstrate the expected purity advantage for X0.

That comparison is not a definitive extractant ranking: the two feeds were independent batches, their measured reaction compositions differed, and wash volumes differed. It could indicate that the dossier is misindexed, that its partition coefficients apply only to the stated reference feed and phase volumes, or that unmodeled species alter extraction. It could also simply reflect process variability. X1 and X3 were not experimentally tested, so their process performance is unidentifiable.

The reactor solvent joined the aqueous-side volume during workup, so solvent volume and extraction phase ratio were coupled. Most later recipes used 0.03 L reaction solvent, 0.03 L added aqueous phase and 0.04 L extractant. Changing any of those volumes would change both reaction concentration and the extraction fraction. The campaign did not independently map that phase-ratio dependence.

## Washing and finishing

Washing should ideally remove impurities preferentially, but it can also remove target. I model one wash schematically as

nP,new = nP,old(1 − lP),
nI,new = nI,old(1 − lI),

where purification requires lI > lP. Multiple washes multiply these retention factors, so an insufficiently selective wash can sharply reduce recovery without delivering specification purity.

The results did not establish a simple monotonic wash-volume law. In S0/C3/330 K/7200 s batches, wash volumes of 0.015, 0.025 and 0.040 L gave final purities of 0.7140, 0.7379 and 0.7338, with recoveries of 0.0533, 0.0527 and 0.0419. These batches support target loss at the largest wash, but their purity differences are too small and confounded by independent reaction feeds to claim a precise effect.

Batch 10 applied two 0.04 L washes to an S2/X2 material. Relative to the one-wash S2 batch 9, recovery fell from 0.0969 to 0.0579, while purity also fell from 0.6652 to 0.6086. Because these were not split aliquots of the same feed, the comparison does not prove that washing decreased purity. It does show that repeating this complete recipe failed to rescue an impurity-rich S2 reaction and incurred substantial recovery loss.

Drying and 600 s concentration reduced liquid volume and prepared the final organic material. In an ideal mass-balance model, concentration removes solvent but not solute and therefore changes concentration rather than solute purity. Any observed product loss could instead arise from volatility, transfer, residual-phase discard, or simulator-specific handling. Those mechanisms were not separately measured.

## Why batch 4 was selected

The governing objective was recovery subject to final purity ≥0.80, not maximum native score or maximum reaction-stage yield. Batch 4 was the only batch clearly above the purity threshold: final purity 0.8395, recovery 0.0428, mass-balance error 0.00305, impurity signal 0.0107 and degradation warning 0.0115. Batch 2 was close but below specification at purity 0.7948, so it was not treated as passing. Several recipes had higher recovery—most notably batch 9 at 0.0969—but failed purity.

The recommended operating sequence is therefore the tested batch-4 process: equal 0.018 mol reagent and component charges, 0.03 L S0, 0.005 mol C3, heating at 350 K for 3600 s with 700 rpm stirring, quenching, adding 0.03 L aqueous phase and 0.04 L X2, mixing for 240 s at 700 rpm, settling for 300 s, selecting the organic phase, washing with 0.03 L, drying, concentrating for 600 s, and assaying the terminated material.

## Scope and unresolved alternatives

This account is empirical and local to the anonymous benchmark materials and tested ranges. Material indices are categories, not chemical identities, so molecular explanations such as ligand electronics or solvent polarity would be invented rather than observed. The data do not identify kinetic rate constants, equilibrium constants under process conditions, reaction orders, the identities of byproducts, or separate losses from extraction, washing, drying and concentration.

The experiment design changed several variables between some batches and provided limited true replication. Consequently, numerical differences should not all be read as causal effects. In particular, the apparent advantages of 330 K/7200 s for reaction yield and of S1/S2 for conversion are credible within the observed recipes, but the exact effect sizes and interactions are uncertain.

Plausible alternative explanations include: a reversible reaction rather than the irreversible network sketched above; catalyst-dependent equilibration; product degradation during heating or workup; solvent-dependent detector response or matrix effects; and phase partitioning that changes with feed composition rather than following constant distribution coefficients. The final-assay conversion values near one in many batches should not be used to reject the earlier HPLC values, because these measurements describe different selected materials and downstream metrics under the stated instrument contract.

A stronger mechanistic study would use split-feed workups to compare extractants and washes on the same reaction mixture, randomized replicate batches to quantify process variance, time-course measurements for C3 in S0, and a factorial catalyst–solvent design. None of those additional data were collected here. The sealed recommendation therefore rests on direct demonstrated specification compliance, while the broader mechanistic explanation remains a constrained, testable interpretation rather than a uniquely identified law.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign: they use C1 at only 0.00025 mol, S2 at 400 K, omit the added component used in my campaign, and include a 0.97 transfer. I therefore used broad predictive intervals that include both final-assay noise and much larger process/model uncertainty. For Q01–Q02, I expect longer heating to increase conversion and recovery, but at 400 K also to increase competing or degradation chemistry, lowering purity. For Q03–Q04, the dossier partition model predicts X0 should sacrifice target recovery but reject impurity more strongly than X2; the campaign’s single confounded X0 comparison did not verify this, so the intervals overlap widely. For Q05–Q06, increasing X2 organic volume should extract more target and thus raise recovery, while co-extracting more impurity and reducing purity. For the low-charge recipes Q07–Q12, the fixed catalyst charge is much larger relative to reagent than in Q01–Q06, so I predict materially greater fractional recovery, although this catalyst-loading extrapolation is especially uncertain. A wash is expected to raise purity and lower recovery (Q08 versus Q07). Two fresh 0.01 L washes should be somewhat more selective, but more product-losing, than one 0.02 L wash (Q10 versus Q09). Concentration should mainly remove solvent, so Q11 and Q12 have nearly identical purity; I allow a small recovery penalty in Q12 for possible handling or concentration loss. All recovery estimates also incorporate the explicit 0.97 transfer fraction.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws tested.** No instance-specific mechanism prior or prediction truth was supplied. The only supplied scientific prior was the incomplete nominal extractant dossier, explicitly described as potentially misindexed.

- The dossier claim that X2 should provide strong target recovery was partly supported: X2 produced all of the better-recovery workups, including batch 9 with recovery 0.0969. However, this was not a controlled extractant comparison.
- The expected purity advantage of X0 was not supported by the available comparison. Batch 8 used X0 and ended at purity 0.4878 and recovery 0.0331, whereas the related S1/X2 batch 7 gave 0.5742 and 0.0788. This changed my view from treating the dossier ranking as a reliable guide to treating it only as a weak prior. The comparison was confounded by independent reaction feeds and different wash volumes, so it did not conclusively contradict the underlying partition coefficients. X1 and X3 remained untested.
- My catalyst claim was supported only locally. Under the common S0, 350 K, 3600 s recipe, C3 in batch 4 outperformed C1 in batch 2 and C2 in batch 3 on final purity: 0.8395 versus 0.7948 and 0.5410. Batch 4 was the evidence that moved C3 from a candidate to the working catalyst. C0 was never tested under the same conditions; batch 1 used a different charge and heating history, so a complete C0 ranking remained untested.
- The proposed temperature–time tradeoff received partial support. Relative to batch 4 at 350 K/3600 s, S0/C3 batches 5, 6 and 12 at 330 K/7200 s had higher HPLC yields, about 0.128–0.130 versus 0.0910. Because both temperature and time changed simultaneously, separate temperature and time laws were not identified.
- The claim that S1 and S2 promote conversion or target formation relative to S0 was supported within C3/330 K recipes. Batches 7–10 had HPLC conversions around 0.436–0.444 and yields 0.207–0.239, compared with conversions 0.211–0.280 and yields near 0.129 in S0 batches 5, 6 and 12. The same experiments changed my judgment by showing that greater upstream yield did not ensure acceptable final purity: batches 7–10 all remained below 0.80 purity.
- A simple law that more washing monotonically increases purity was contradicted or at least not resolved. S0 batches 5, 6 and 12 used 0.015, 0.025 and 0.040 L washes but gave purities 0.7140, 0.7379 and 0.7338. The two-wash S2 recipe in batch 10 had lower purity and recovery than the one-wash batch 9. Since these were independent feeds, the evidence chiefly rejects confident use of a monotonic law rather than proving that washing intrinsically lowers purity.
- The equilibrium partition equations, the competing-pathway reaction network, and the assumption that concentration ideally preserves solute amounts were explanatory models rather than identified laws. No campaign experiment isolated their parameters. Every later batch used concentration, neither phase was comprehensively assayed before disposal, and no true kinetic time series was collected.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would perform a prespecified split-feed study from one homogeneous S2/C3 reaction mixture, because the leading explanation for batches 7–10 is that S1/S2 created an impurity-rich upstream feed that ordinary washing could not rescue. The principal alternative is that these solvents produced an adequate feed but the chosen extraction/washing process caused the poor final selectivity.

I would use the batch-9 upstream recipe, assay the quenched homogeneous feed once, then divide it equally into matched containers. One arm would receive the batch-9 X2 workup; the other would receive a deliberately more selective workup, such as lower organic-to-aqueous ratio and staged washing. Both arms would be processed and assayed identically otherwise. This is one split-feed experiment rather than two unrelated batches, so feed variability would not confound the workup comparison.

If both arms remained below 0.80 purity with similar target-to-impurity behavior, especially when the quenched-feed assay was already impurity rich, I would strengthen the upstream co-production explanation and stop trying to rescue S2 solely through washing. If the selective arm crossed 0.80 with an acceptable recovery while the standard arm reproduced batch 9, I would shift toward the workup-limited alternative. If purity improved only by a very large recovery loss, I would retain a mixed explanation: upstream selectivity is inadequate, but partitioning can trade recovery for compliance. A failure to reproduce batch 9 would instead raise process variability as the leading explanation.

3. **Unused evidence and reliability.** I did not inspect or fit the raw HPLC/final-assay spectral artifacts, replicate traces, peak assignments, or calibration residuals. I mainly used processed estimates. I also did not assay both aqueous and organic phases, so discarded target and impurity amounts were not directly measured. Intermediate mass balances, solvent-loss behavior, and target loss during drying, concentration and transfer were therefore not separately identified. Final-assay fields such as near-unity conversion were not used as direct continuations of upstream HPLC conversion because the instrument contract warned that stage-specific metrics need not assay the same material. Cost, native score and most timing/safety data were also secondary to the stated purity-constrained recovery goal.

Batch 1 supplied little clean causal evidence because it differed in charge, temperature and heating sequence. Comparisons involving wash volume, X0 versus X2, or reaction solvent were not true randomized replicates and therefore support direction more strongly than effect size.

The sealed batch-4 recommendation is empirically grounded but still based on a single passing run. Its purity of 0.8395 is only about 0.04 above the threshold, and no exact replicate established process robustness. Thus its transferability and expected pass probability are less reliable than the statement that it was the best observed compliant batch.

The least reliable blind predictions are those for Q07–Q12, because their 0.002 mol charge and catalyst-to-reagent ratio were far outside my campaign experience. Q01–Q06 are also uncertain because 400 K, 0.00025 mol C1, omission of the added component, and the explicit transfer operation were not jointly tested. Predicted contrasts for extractant, wash staging and concentration rely heavily on generic partition/process reasoning rather than directly identified laws.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because recovery counted only after satisfying purity ≥0.80, I prioritized completing full workups and final assays and searched for a passing recipe. That strategy found batch 4 but sacrificed clean factorial comparisons, split-feed workups, kinetic time courses and exact replication. There was no clear conflict with the goal, but the specification-first search produced stronger evidence for selecting an observed batch than for identifying a general mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 4 was the only completed batch with final-assay purity clearly at or above the required 0.80 (0.8395), while retaining recovery 0.0428. Batch 2 was below threshold at 0.7948, and batches with greater recovery also failed purity; therefore batch 4 best satisfies the specification-first objective.
